meta.title: Who really said "Most people do not listen with the intent to understand; they listen with the intent to reply"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Stephen Covey wrote it. It is Habit 5 of The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), p. 239. Often confused with a line by Roy T. Bennett.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Most people do not listen with the intent to understand; they listen with the intent to reply'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Covey, and placeable: Habit 5 of The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), p. 239. What travels badly is the wording, not the name.

answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and unusually easy to place. The sentence appears in Habit 5, “Seek First to Understand, Then to Be Understood,” of The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People, first published by Simon and Schuster in 1989. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ files it under that book and gives p. 239, and the two sentences that follow it in the book are reproduced verbatim in Covey’s own later compilations.

source.excerpt: Most people do not listen with the intent to understand; they listen with the intent to reply. They’re either speaking or preparing to speak.
trail: Wikiquote’s Stephen Covey page ↗ carries the line in its sourced material, under the heading The Seven Habits Of Highly Effective People (1989), with the citation “p. 239.” It is not in that page’s Disputed or Misattributed sections.

Full-text search of digitised books at Open Library ↗ returns the sentence with its neighbours intact — the preceding “We typically seek first to be understood” and the following “They’re either speaking or preparing to speak” — including inside Covey’s own later collections Daily Reflections for Highly Effective People and The Wisdom and Teachings of Stephen R. Covey.
The 1989 first edition is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗ as Simon and Schuster, New York, 1989, ISBN 0671663984, 366 pages. The scan is borrow-only, so the page image cannot be quoted here.

Goodreads’ most-shared copy of the line ↗ gives the same wording and names the same book under its later subtitle, Powerful Lessons in Personal Change. Quote Investigator has no article on this quotation — nothing about it has needed disentangling.
source.excerptNote: The passage continues past these two sentences — Covey goes on to describe people filtering everything through their own paradigms — but the book is in copyright, so only the quoted sentence and the line that follows it are reproduced here.

source.rightsNote: The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People was first published in 1989 by Simon and Schuster, so it sits firmly inside US copyright — nothing published in 1931 or later has aged into the public domain. Quoting the sentence to identify and discuss it is ordinary fair use; reproducing the surrounding passage at length is not, which is why only the quoted line and the short sentence after it appear above.

author.heading: Stephen R. Covey
author.metaLine: 1932–2012 · American educator, author and leadership consultant
author.bio: Stephen R. Covey was born in Salt Lake City on 24 October 1932, took an MBA at Harvard Business School and a doctorate in religious education at Brigham Young University, and taught business and organisational behaviour before becoming one of the most widely read management writers of the late twentieth century. The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People, published in 1989, made him a global fixture in corporate training and turned a set of essentially moral arguments about character into a business bestseller. He was later a professor at Utah State University’s Jon M. Huntsman School of Business, and died in Idaho Falls on 16 July 2012.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The name on this quotation is right — it really is Covey’s sentence, in his own bestselling book. What travels badly is the wording, and one near-twin written by somebody else entirely.

items.why: Bennett’s The Light in the Heart contains a separate passage making the same point in different words — “we don’t listen to understand. We listen to reply” — and it sits, sourced to Bennett, on Goodreads’ page of quotes from that book ↗. Online the two lines are routinely swapped, so Covey’s sentence gets Bennett’s name and Bennett’s gets Covey’s.

items.who: “we listen with the intent to reply”
items.why: Covey wrote it in the third person, as a diagnosis of what most people do. A softened first-person rewrite is in print too: full-text search of digitised books ↗ turns it up as “we listen with the intent to reply. We are either speaking or preparing…” in William L. Ewens’s Unfolding Ourselves.

The 1989 first edition is subtitled Restoring the Character Ethic; later printings carry Powerful Lessons in Personal Change, which is the subtitle Goodreads attaches to the quotation ↗. They are the same book, not two sources — but citations that mix them look like a provenance problem when there isn’t one.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Stephen Covey’s, from Habit 5 of The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989) — Wikiquote’s sourced entry puts it at p. 239 ↗.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: Covey builds Habit 5 — “Seek First to Understand, Then to Be Understood” — on a small and slightly uncomfortable observation about what we are actually doing while someone else is talking. His answer is that we are queueing up our own reply and filtering what we hear through our own experience rather than the speaker’s. The remedy he proposes is empathic listening: listening to understand the other person’s frame, not to win the exchange.

That one sentence has comfortably outlived the framework around it. It turns up on sales-training slides, in therapy waiting rooms and at school assemblies, usually with nothing but a surname attached — which is a pity, because unlike most viral one-liners this one has a book, a chapter and a page behind it.
context.detailsSummary: Editions, pagination and the rest of the passage
detailsBody: Pagination is the only soft spot. Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ gives p. 239, and the same page number turns up independently in a separate leadership text that quotes the identical passage. But Covey’s book has been reset for paperback and anniversary editions many times since 1989, so a copy on your shelf will not necessarily land the sentence on 239.

The passage does not stop at the famous sentence. In the book it runs on into “They’re either speaking or preparing to speak” and then a line about reading your own autobiography into other people’s lives — wording that is reproduced in Covey’s own later collections and is searchable at Open Library ↗.
context.pull: Unlike most viral one-liners, this one has a book, a chapter and a page behind it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section for Stephen Covey lists "Most people do not listen with the intent to understand; they listen with the intent to reply." under the heading The Seven Habits Of Highly Effective People (1989) with the citation p. 239; the page's other sections are Disputed and Misattributed, and this line is in neither.

The Internet Archive holds a scan of the 1989 first edition: The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People: Restoring the Character Ethic, Stephen R. Covey, Simon and Schuster, New York, 1989, ISBN 0671663984, 366 pages, access-restricted (borrow only).
Internet Archive item metadata for sevenhabitshigly00cove gives publisher 'New York : Simon and Schuster', year 1989, ISBN 0671663984, creator 'Covey, Stephen R'.

Open Library full-text search for "they listen with the intent to reply" returns matches in many digitised books, including Stephen R. Covey's own The Wisdom and Teachings of Stephen R Covey, which shows the continuation 'They're either speaking or preparing to speak. They're filtering everything through their own paradigms, reading their autobiography into other people's lives.'

Open Library full-text search for "we listen with the intent to reply" returns a first-person rewrite of Covey's sentence in print — 'listen with the intent to understand; we listen with the intent to reply. We are either speaking or preparing…' — in William L. Ewens's Unfolding Ourselves.

Goodreads displays the quotation exactly as "Most people do not listen with the intent to understand; they listen with the intent to reply." attributed to Stephen R. Covey and sourced to The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People: Powerful Lessons in Personal Change.

Goodreads' quotes page for Roy T. Bennett's The Light in the Heart carries the separate, similar passage: 'Listen with curiosity. Speak with honesty. Act with integrity. The greatest problem with communication is we don't listen to understand. We listen to reply…' attributed to Bennett.

Wikipedia records Stephen Covey as born 24 October 1932 in Salt Lake City, Utah, died 16 July 2012 in Idaho Falls, Idaho; an American educator, author, businessman and speaker with an MBA from Harvard Business School and a Doctor of Religious Education from Brigham Young University; The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People was published in 1989.
Wikipedia gives The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People a first publication year of 1989 and names Habit 5 as 'Seek first to understand, then to be understood'.
Open Library's search API records first_publish_year 1989 for The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People by Stephen R. Covey.
